claim: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3) is the most frequent dominant ataxia worldwide.
source: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3; also known as Machado-Joseph disease) is the most frequent dominant ataxia worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement from the introduction that cites established knowledge about SCA3 prevalence.

claim: SCA3 is caused by CAG repeat expansion in the gene ATXN3 that is normally 12–42 repeats long but is expanded to ~60–87 repeats in patients.
source: SCA3 is caused by CAG repeat expansion in the gene ATXN3 that is normally 12–42 repeats long but is expanded to ~60–87 repeats in patients (Todi et al., 2007b; Costa and Paulson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The CAG triplet repeat encodes a polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the protein, ataxin-3.
source: This triplet repeat encodes a polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the protein, ataxin-3, a deubiquitinase (DUB; Figure 1) implicated in protein quality control and DNA repair (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is established knowledge about the genetic code.

claim: Ataxin-3 is a deubiquitinase implicated in protein quality control and DNA repair.
source: This triplet repeat encodes a polyglutamine (polyQ) tract in the protein, ataxin-3, a deubiquitinase (DUB; Figure 1) implicated in protein quality control and DNA repair (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are nine neurodegenerative disorders caused by abnormal polyQ expansion in diverse proteins.
source: SCA3 is one of the nine neurodegenerative disorders caused by abnormal polyQ expansion in diverse proteins (Todi et al., 2007b; Costa and Paulson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The polyQ family includes Huntington's disease (HD), SCAs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 17, Dentatorubral–pallidoluysian atrophy, and Kennedy's disease.
source: The polyQ family includes Huntington's disease (HD), SCAs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 17, Dentatorubral–pallidoluysian atrophy, and Kennedy's disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polyQ diseases.

claim: HD and SCA3 are the two most common among the nine known polyQ diseases.
source: Together, HD and SCA3 are the two most common among the nine known polyQ diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about disease prevalence.

claim: Although each polyQ disorder is caused by the aberrant lengthening of the same domain, they are clinically distinct diseases.
source: Although each polyQ disorder is caused by the aberrant lengthening of the same domain, they are clinically distinct diseases (Todi et al., 2007b; Costa and Paulson, 2012; Nath and Lieberman, 2017; Pérez Ortiz and Orr, 2018; Lieberman et al., 2019; Klockgether et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Protein context (regions outside of the polyQ) modulates the properties of the elongated tract in polyQ disorders.
source: Fundamental to polyQ disorders is the role of protein context, i.e. regions outside of the polyQ that modulate the properties of the elongated tract (Todi et al., 2007b; Nath and Lieberman, 2017; Pérez Ortiz and Orr, 2018; Lieberman et al., 2019; Klockgether et al., 2019; Blount et al., 2014; Ristic et al., 2018; Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Protein context differentiates polyQ diseases.
source: It is the protein context that differentiates polyQ diseases; why, for example, expansions in ataxin-3 cause SCA3 instead of another disorder.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different polyQ proteins cause different diseases.

claim: In SCA1, the nuclear localization signal directs ataxin-1 to the nucleus and is necessary for pathogenesis.
source: For instance, in SCA1, the nuclear localization signal directs its disease protein, ataxin-1, to the nucleus and is necessary for pathogenesis (Pérez Ortiz and Orr, 2018; Klement et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ataxin-3 contains a ubiquitin-protease (Josephin) domain on its N-terminal half.
source: Ataxin-3 contains a ubiquitin-protease (Josephin) domain on its N-terminal half (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Josephin domain contains the catalytic triad that enables ataxin-3 to cleave ubiquitin bonds.
source: Within it are the catalytic triad that enables ataxin-3 to cleave ubiquitin bonds, as well as two ubiquitin-binding sites (UbS) that either interact with ubiquitin (UbS1), or with ubiquitin and the proteasome-associated protein, Rad23 (UbS2; Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UbS1 interacts with ubiquitin.
source: Within it are the catalytic triad that enables ataxin-3 to cleave ubiquitin bonds, as well as two ubiquitin-binding sites (UbS) that either interact with ubiquitin (UbS1), or with ubiquitin and the proteasome-associated protein, Rad23 (UbS2; Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UbS2 interacts with ubiquitin and the proteasome-associated protein, Rad23.
source: Within it are the catalytic triad that enables ataxin-3 to cleave ubiquitin bonds, as well as two ubiquitin-binding sites (UbS) that either interact with ubiquitin (UbS1), or with ubiquitin and the proteasome-associated protein, Rad23 (UbS2; Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ataxin-3 contains two ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs 1 and 2) downstream of the Josephin domain.
source: Downstream are two ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs 1 and 2), followed by a site that binds the AAA ATPase, VCP (VCP-binding motif; VBM), and the polyQ tract (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ataxin-3 contains a VCP-binding motif (VBM) followed by the polyQ tract.
source: Downstream are two ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs 1 and 2), followed by a site that binds the AAA ATPase, VCP (VCP-binding motif; VBM), and the polyQ tract (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ataxin-3 contains a third UIM (UIM3) at the C-terminus.
source: At the end resides a third UIM (UIM3) (Costa and Paulson, 2012; Dantuma and Herzog, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In a less common isoform, UIM3 is replaced by a hydrophobic C-terminus.
source: In another, less common isoform UIM3 is replaced by a hydrophobic C-terminus (Johnson et al., 2019; Harris et al., 2010; Kawaguchi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UIMs enable ataxin-3 to bind poly-ubiquitin.
source: UIMs enable ataxin-3 to bind poly-ubiquitin (Winborn et al., 2008; Todi et al., 2009; Todi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UbS2 regulates ataxin-3 turnover and toxicity.
source: UbS2 regulates ataxin-3 turnover and toxicity (Blount et al., 2014; Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The VBM controls ataxin-3 aggregation and toxicity, but not turnover.
source: the VBM controls ataxin-3 aggregation and toxicity, but not turnover (Blount et al., 2014; Ristic et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2015a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The catalytic site is necessary for ataxin-3's inherent neuroprotective functions.
source: and the catalytic site is necessary for ataxin-3's inherent neuroprotective functions (Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a; Tsou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Adult, pan-neuronal expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact domains caused early lethality.
source: Adult, pan-neuronal expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact domains caused early lethality (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Catalytically inactive ataxin-3 led to significantly shorter lifespan compared to intact ataxin-3.
source: Catalytically inactive ataxin-3 led to significantly shorter lifespan, as did the version with mutated UbS2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ataxin-3 with mutated UbS2 led to significantly shorter lifespan compared to intact ataxin-3.
source: Catalytically inactive ataxin-3 led to significantly shorter lifespan, as did the version with mutated UbS2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutating the VBM led to markedly longer lifespan compared to intact ataxin-3.
source: Mutating the VBM led to markedly longer lifespan compared to 'intact'.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM did not reach normal longevity.
source: Still, flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM did not reach normal longevity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 'intact' showed reduced motility.
source: We observed reduced motility with flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 'intact' and further impaired motility with those expressing inactive ataxin-3 or ataxin-3 with mutated UbS2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies expressing inactive ataxin-3 or ataxin-3 with mutated UbS2 showed further impaired motility compared to intact ataxin-3.
source: We observed reduced motility with flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 'intact' and further impaired motility with those expressing inactive ataxin-3 or ataxin-3 with mutated UbS2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM did not significantly impact motility.
source: On the other hand, pan-neuronal expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM did not significantly impact motility.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In glial cells, catalytically inactive and UbS2-mutated ataxin-3 led to increased toxicity compared with pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact domains.
source: Overall trends were similar to neuronal cells: catalytically inactive and UbS2-mutated ataxin-3 led to increased toxicity compared with pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact domains.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In glial cells, there was a statistical difference in toxicity between pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated catalytic site and the one with mutated UbS2.
source: But, unlike in neurons, in glial cells we did observe a statistical difference in toxicity between pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated catalytic site and the one with mutated UbS2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no statistical difference in longevity between controls not expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 and flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM in glial cells.
source: There was no statistical difference between controls not expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 and flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM both in terms of longevity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and motility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no statistical difference in motility between controls not expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 and flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM in glial cells.
source: There was no statistical difference between controls not expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 and flies expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated VBM both in terms of longevity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and motility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Domains outside of ataxin-3's polyQ play significant modulatory roles in pathogenicity.
source: Based on these collective data, we conclude that domains outside of ataxin-3's polyQ play significant modulatory roles in pathogenicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The isolated polyQ80 was more toxic than full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 when expressed in all tissues or only in neurons.
source: The isolated polyQ80 was more toxic than full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 when expressed in all tissues or only in neurons (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: In glia, full-length ataxin-3 was more problematic than polyQ80.
source: This pattern was reversed in glia; full-length ataxin-3 was more problematic than polyQ80 in these cells, highlighting a need to better understand glial response to polyQ proteins.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: PolyQ80 was generally less toxic than the same peptide with appended UIMs when expressed everywhere, selectively in neurons, or in glia.
source: Intriguingly, polyQ80 was generally less toxic than the same peptide with appended UIMs when expressed everywhere, selectively in neurons, or in glia; addition of UIM3 appeared particularly pathogenic (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Addition of UIM3 to polyQ80 appeared particularly pathogenic.
source: Intriguingly, polyQ80 was generally less toxic than the same peptide with appended UIMs when expressed everywhere, selectively in neurons, or in glia; addition of UIM3 appeared particularly pathogenic (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Eye-restricted expression of polyQ80 with UIM3 was more problematic than the isolated polyQ80 or polyQ80 with all UIMs.
source: Eye-restricted expression of these transgenes also led to variable toxicity, with UIM3 addition being more problematic than the isolated polyQ80 or polyQ80 with all UIMs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PolyQ80 was noticeably less toxic than versions with UIMs when expressed pan-neuronally only in adults.
source: PolyQ80 was noticeably less toxic than versions with UIMs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Flies expressing Q80-UIM3 or UIM1-2-Q80 lived longer than those expressing polyQ80 with all UIMs.
source: Flies expressing Q80-UIM3 or UIM1-2-Q80 lived longer than those expressing polyQ80 with all UIMs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: UIMs regulate the pathogenicity of the expanded polyQ of ataxin-3.
source: Collectively, data in Figure 2 indicate a regulatory role for UIMs in the pathogenicity of the expanded polyQ of ataxin-3, and led us to explore them in the full-length protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated UIMs was consistently and markedly less toxic than its counterpart with intact UIMs in all of the tissues tested.
source: Expression of pathogenic ataxin-3 with mutated UIMs was consistently and markedly less toxic than its counterpart with intact UIMs in all of the tissues tested (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Adults expressing UIM-mutated ataxin-3 retained mobility longer than adults expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs.
source: Motility assays also showed that adults expressing UIM-mutated ataxin-3 retained mobility longer than adults expressing pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutating the UIMs renders ataxin-3 significantly less pathogenic.
source: We conclude that mutating its UIMs renders ataxin-3 significantly less pathogenic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Mutating the UIMs does not cause loss of ataxin-3 protein.
source: Mutating the UIMs does not cause loss of ataxin-3 protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no significant difference in subcellular distribution between ataxin-3 with intact or mutated UIMs.
source: Based on subcellular fractionation, there was no significant difference in distribution between ataxin-3 with intact or mutated UIMs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutating the UIMs rendered pathogenic ataxin-3 less aggregation-prone.
source: However, according to two different assays, mutating the UIMs rendered pathogenic ataxin-3 less aggregation-prone.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Centrifugation-based protocols showed higher aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs.
source: Centrifugation-based protocols and filter-trap assays both showed higher aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Filter-trap assays showed higher aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs.
source: Centrifugation-based protocols and filter-trap assays both showed higher aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 and other polyQ proteins precedes toxicity in Drosophila studies.
source: In our Drosophila studies, aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 and other polyQ proteins precedes toxicity; also, the level of aggregation mirrors the extent of their pathogenicity (Ristic et al., 2018; Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a; Johnson et al., 2019; Tsou et al., 2013; Tsou et al., 2015b; Tsou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The level of aggregation mirrors the extent of pathogenicity of pathogenic ataxin-3 and other polyQ proteins in Drosophila studies.
source: In our Drosophila studies, aggregation of pathogenic ataxin-3 and other polyQ proteins precedes toxicity; also, the level of aggregation mirrors the extent of their pathogenicity (Ristic et al., 2018; Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a; Johnson et al., 2019; Tsou et al., 2013; Tsou et al., 2015b; Tsou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The UIMs of pathogenic ataxin-3 enhance its aggregation and toxicity in Drosophila.
source: Based on data from Figures 3 and 4, we conclude that the UIMs of pathogenic ataxin-3 enhance its aggregation and toxicity in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The UIMs of ataxin-3 bind poly-ubiquitin.
source: The UIMs of ataxin-3 indeed bind poly-ubiquitin (Winborn et al., 2008; Todi et al., 2009; Todi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified heat shock protein cognate 4 (Hsc70-4) only in the presence of ataxin-3 with intact UIMs.
source: Mass spectrometry from the dissected regions yielded heat shock protein cognate 4 (Hsc70-4) only in the presence of ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 co-immunoprecipitated endogenous Hsc70-4 in a UIM-dependent manner.
source: Full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 co-IP-ed endogenous Hsc70-4 in a UIM-dependent manner: whereas pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs co-IP-ed Hsc70-4, we did not observe the same with UIM-mutated, pathogenic ataxin-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs co-immunoprecipitated Hsc70-4.
source: Full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 co-IP-ed endogenous Hsc70-4 in a UIM-dependent manner: whereas pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs co-IP-ed Hsc70-4, we did not observe the same with UIM-mutated, pathogenic ataxin-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: UIM-mutated, pathogenic ataxin-3 did not co-immunoprecipitate Hsc70-4.
source: Full-length, pathogenic ataxin-3 co-IP-ed endogenous Hsc70-4 in a UIM-dependent manner: whereas pathogenic ataxin-3 with intact UIMs co-IP-ed Hsc70-4, we did not observe the same with UIM-mutated, pathogenic ataxin-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The interaction of ataxin-3 with Hsc70-4 could potentially rely more heavily on UIM3.
source: The interaction of ataxin-3 with Hsc70-4 could potentially rely more heavily on UIM3.
evidence: This is inferred from co-IP data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: PolyQ80-UIM3 co-immunoprecipitated endogenous Hsc70-4 more readily than polyQ80 alone or polyQ80 with UIMs 1 and 2.
source: PolyQ80-UIM3 co-IP-ed endogenous Hsc70-4 more readily than polyQ80 alone or polyQ80 with UIMs 1 and 2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All three polyQ80 versions co-immunoprecipitated Hsc70-4, but UIM3 appeared more important than the two other UIMs in facilitating an interaction.
source: All three polyQ80 versions co-IP-ed Hsc70-4, but UIM3 appeared more important than the two other UIMs in facilitating an interaction.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The UIMs of ataxin-3 are an interaction site for Hsc70-4 in vivo.
source: Collectively, these results highlight the UIMs of ataxin-3 as an interaction site for Hsc70-4 in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Hsc70-4 belongs to the heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) superfamily.
source: Hsc70-4 belongs to the heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) superfamily.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein families.

claim: The closest human ortholog of Hsc70-4 is the constitutively expressed, heat shock protein family A member 8 (HSPA8).
source: Its closest human ortholog is the constitutively expressed, heat shock protein family A member 8 (HSPA8; Takayama et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The primary role of Hsc70-4 is that of an ATP-dependent chaperone for unfolded proteins in protein quality control.
source: Alongside other HSP70 members, its primary role is that of an ATP-dependent chaperone for unfolded proteins in protein quality control (Yamamoto et al., 2010; Grove et al., 2011; Goodwin et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Sopha et al., 2012; Robert et al., 2019; Loeffler, 2019; Abildgaard et al., 2020; Davis et al., 2020; Faust and Rosenzweig, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: HSPA8 is a part of the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation system.
source: HSPA8 is a part of the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation system and is also involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy (Robert et al., 2019; Loeffler, 2019; Stricher et al., 2013; Kampinga and Bergink, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HSPA8 is involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy.
source: HSPA8 is a part of the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation system and is also involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy (Robert et al., 2019; Loeffler, 2019; Stricher et al., 2013; Kampinga and Bergink, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hsc70-4 is a different member of the HSP70 superfamily than fly Hsc70Cb and human HSPA1L.
source: Hsc70-4 is a different member of the HSP70 superfamily than fly Hsc70Cb and human HSPA1L, both of which were previously reported to suppress polyQ-dependent degeneration (Warrick et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2010; Iijima-Ando et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fly Hsc70Cb and human HSPA1L were previously reported to suppress polyQ-dependent degeneration.
source: Hsc70-4 is a different member of the HSP70 superfamily than fly Hsc70Cb and human HSPA1L, both of which were previously reported to suppress polyQ-dependent degeneration (Warrick et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2010; Iijima-Ando et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Widespread targeting of Hsc70-4 in the fly was developmentally lethal.
source: We selected fly eyes because widespread targeting of Hsc70-4 in the fly was developmentally lethal (larval, pupal, and pharate adult lethality), whereas expression in fly eyes was not problematic (clearly present pseudopupil and good overall morphology).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: Expression of Hsc70-4 RNAi in fly eyes was not problematic.
source: We selected fly eyes because widespread targeting of Hsc70-4 in the fly was developmentally lethal (larval, pupal, and pharate adult lethality), whereas expression in fly eyes was not problematic (clearly present pseudopupil and good overall morphology).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: Expression of each Hsc70-4 RNAi line in fly eyes led to reduced Hsc70-4 levels.
source: Expression of each line in fly eyes led to reduced Hsc70-4 levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hsc70-4 knockdown consistently improved eye phenotype caused by pathogenic ataxin-3.
source: Hsc70-4 knockdown consistently improved eye phenotype, denoted by the persistence of the pseudopupil − an indicator of underlying structure integrity − and fewer cases with depigmentation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both SDS-resistant ataxin-3 species and aggregates isolated by filter-trap assays were reduced in the presence of Hsc70-4 RNAi.
source: Both SDS-resistant ataxin-3 species and aggregates isolated by filter-trap assays were reduced in the presence of Hsc70-4 RNAi (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: Suppression of eye phenotypes by Hsc70-4 knockdown is likely a consequence of reduced SCA3 protein aggregation.
source: Since aggregation of ataxin-3 is a key determinant of its toxicity in flies (Ristic et al., 2018; Sutton et al., 2017; Tsou et al., 2015a; Johnson et al., 2019), suppression of eye phenotypes by Hsc70-4 knockdown is likely a consequence of reduced SCA3 protein aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior observations and current data.

claim: Knocking down Hsc70-4 did not have a detectable impact on eye phenotype caused by pathogenic ataxin-3(UIM*).
source: Lastly, we tested the effect of Hsc70-4 knockdown on eye phenotypes from ataxin-3 with mutated UIMs. Knocking down Hsc70-4 did not have a detectable impact on eye phenotype caused by pathogenic ataxin-3(UIM*) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Hsc70-4 is an enhancer of pathogenic ataxin-3 toxicity in a manner dependent on UIMs.
source: Collectively, these data highlight Hsc70-4 as an enhancer of pathogenic ataxin-3 toxicity in a manner dependent on UIMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of polyQ80 led to pseudopupil loss and depigmentation.
source: Expression of polyQ80 led to pseudopupil loss and depigmentation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of Hsc70-4 improved depigmentation caused by polyQ80, even though it did not recover the pseudopupil.
source: Knockdown of Hsc70-4 improved depigmentation, even though it did not recover the pseudopupil, indicative of ameliorated pathology (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Improved eye phenotype from Hsc70-4 knockdown was accompanied by reduced polyQ80 aggregates.
source: Importantly, improved eye phenotype was accompanied by reduced polyQ80 aggregates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Hsc70-4 knockdown has a protective effect in a polyQ78 model.
source: We confirmed a protective effect from Hsc70-4 knockdown in yet another polyQ model (Warrick et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When Hsc70-4 was knocked down in the polyQ78 model, the ommatidia were visible in a clear sign of toxicity suppression.
source: When Hsc70-4 was knocked down, the ommatidia were visible in a clear sign of toxicity suppression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Hsc70-4 may have a wider role as an enhancer of toxicity from different polyQ proteins.
source: Altogether, these results suggest the possibility of a wider role for Hsc70-4 as an enhancer of toxicity from different polyQ proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Ataxin-3 proteins bind each other.
source: Ataxin-3 proteins bind each other (Ellisdon et al., 2006; Todi et al., 2007a; Masino et al., 2004; Masino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The UIMs were important, but not necessary, for inter-ataxin-3 interactions.
source: We found that the UIMs were important, but not necessary, for these interactions; a reduced amount of full-length, V5-tagged pathogenic ataxin-3 co-IP-ed with UIM* ataxin-3 compared to ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A reduced amount of full-length, V5-tagged pathogenic ataxin-3 co-immunoprecipitated with UIM* ataxin-3 compared to ataxin-3 with intact UIMs.
source: We found that the UIMs were important, but not necessary, for these interactions; a reduced amount of full-length, V5-tagged pathogenic ataxin-3 co-IP-ed with UIM* ataxin-3 compared to ataxin-3 with intact UIMs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: UIM3 is more important for inter-ataxin-3 interaction than UIMs 1 and 2.
source: Additional co-IPs using truncated polyQ fragments and ataxin-3 with a wild-type polyQ indicated that UIM3 is more important for this interaction than UIMs 1 and 2 (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 8B.
